clinicalPearls: Scoliosis arising from congenital vertebral anomalies present from birth, caused by errors in the embryonic formation and segmentation of the vertebrae

The anomalies are classified as failure of formation (for example a hemivertebra), failure of segmentation (for example a unilateral unsegmented bar), or a mixed pattern, and the combination determines the growth imbalance
A unilateral unsegmented bar with a contralateral hemivertebra is the most progressive combination because growth is tethered on one side and unopposed on the other
Because the vertebrae, heart, and kidneys form at the same embryonic stage, congenital scoliosis carries frequent VACTERL-type associations, so cardiac and renal evaluation is essential
Intraspinal anomalies such as tethered cord, diastematomyelia, and syrinx are common, making whole-spine magnetic resonance imaging a routine part of assessment
Serial standing radiographs with Cobb-angle measurement track progression, which depends on the type of anomaly and the growth remaining rather than on bracing responsiveness
Bracing is generally ineffective for the primary structural curve, and progressive deformity is treated surgically, sometimes with early growth-preserving techniques
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital scoliosis results from anomalous development of the vertebral column during the first weeks of embryogenesis, producing asymmetric vertebral growth that drives a lateral curve. Failure of formation leaves a wedge or hemivertebra with deficient bone on one side, while failure of segmentation leaves vertebrae fused by a bar that prevents growth on that side; either imbalance, and especially their combination, causes the spine to curve as it grows. Because vertebral segmentation coincides with development of the cardiac and renal systems and the neural tube, the same insult frequently produces associated cardiac, renal, and intraspinal anomalies, the basis of the VACTERL association and of the high rate of cord tethering and dysraphism.
additionalDifferentials: Syndromic scoliosis, for example in neurofibromatosis or a connective-tissue disorder
Scoliosis from an intraspinal anomaly such as diastematomyelia or tethered cord
Spondylocostal or spondylothoracic dysostosis with multiple segmentation defects
Curve associated with a spinal tumour or infection
additionalInvestigations: Standing posteroanterior and lateral whole-spine radiographs with Cobb-angle measurement and serial monitoring
Whole-spine magnetic resonance imaging to define intraspinal anomalies such as tethered cord or diastematomyelia
Renal ultrasound to screen for the frequently associated urinary-tract anomalies
Echocardiography to detect associated congenital cardiac lesions
Computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction to characterise the vertebral anomaly before surgery
Neurological examination and assessment for other VACTERL-associated malformations
redFlags: A unilateral unsegmented bar with a contralateral hemivertebra, the most progressive pattern
Neurological signs indicating cord tethering, diastematomyelia, or other intraspinal anomaly
Associated cardiac or renal anomalies within a VACTERL pattern
Rapid curve progression, especially during periods of accelerated growth
Cutaneous markers of spinal dysraphism such as a hairy patch, dimple, or naevus over the spine
reference.prognosis: The outlook depends on the specific anomaly, as balanced defects may progress little while a unilateral bar with a contralateral hemivertebra progresses relentlessly; early recognition and timely surgery can control progression, but associated cardiac, renal, and neural anomalies also influence overall prognosis.
pitfalls: Failing to screen for cardiac and renal anomalies given the VACTERL association
Omitting magnetic resonance imaging and missing a tethered cord or diastematomyelia before surgery
Relying on bracing for a structural congenital curve that will not respond
Underestimating the progressive potential of a unilateral unsegmented bar
Delaying surgical intervention until the deformity and any compensatory curve are advanced
management: Monitor balanced or low-risk curves with serial standing radiographs and Cobb-angle measurement, since progression is driven by the anomaly type and remaining growth

Offer surgical correction for progressive curves — hemivertebra excision, convex growth arrest, or growth-friendly instrumentation such as growing rods in the young child, and instrumented fusion once growth is complete
Address intraspinal anomalies (tethered cord, diastematomyelia, syrinx) identified on whole-spine MRI with neurosurgical release before undertaking deformity correction
Screen for and manage the frequently associated VACTERL anomalies, including echocardiography for cardiac lesions and renal ultrasound for urinary-tract anomalies
Recognise that bracing is largely ineffective for the rigid congenital curve itself and is reserved for accompanying flexible compensatory curves
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary team of paediatric spinal surgery, neurosurgery, cardiology and nephrology
